chunks: And with this chain of narrators, he said:

Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) said: 'If a servant could see his appointed term of death and the speed with which it is approaching him, he would hate his aspirations and abandon the pursuit of the world.'

key_terms.أَجَل: Appointed term of death or lifespan
key_terms.الْعَبْد: The servant (of God), referring to a person

ai.seo_question: How does contemplating death help a Muslim detach from worldly desires?
ai.summary: In this tradition from *Uyun Akhbar al-Rida*, Imam Ali (a.s.) links the psychological state of 'amal' (worldly hope) directly to the inevitability of death, suggesting that true awareness of one's appointed term (*ajal*) naturally extinguishes the desire for temporal pursuits. This teaching aligns with the Shia concept of *zuhd* (asceticism) not as mere renunciation, but as a conscious detachment rooted in the certainty of the Hereafter, a theme frequently elaborated by Shaykh al-Saduq to illustrate the spiritual maturity of the Imams.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: Ali ibn Abi Talib (a.s.) said, “If a servant (i.e. a person) could see his death and the speed with which it is approaching him he would hate his aspirations and abandon worldly desires.”
